short: It eliminated the Scottish king and aristocracy, securing England's northern border.
full:
On 9 September 1513, an English army led by the Earl of Surrey intercepted an invading Scottish force at Flodden in Northumberland. King James IV of Scotland had crossed the border in support of his French allies, honouring the Auld Alliance after Henry VIII invaded France. The Scottish army was heavily armed but their pike formations proved unwieldy on the wet, uneven ground.

The English deployed shorter, more versatile bills, which proved devastating in close combat. The battle resulted in a catastrophic defeat for Scotland. James IV was killed, alongside several bishops, eleven earls, fifteen lords, and an estimated ten thousand men. His death left the infant James V on the throne, plunging Scotland into a prolonged period of minority rule and political instability. The destruction of the Scottish political class effectively neutralized the northern threat to England for a generation, allowing Henry VIII to pursue his continental ambitions without fear of an immediate rearguard attack.
